prompt.context: Your client is the director of the collections division of a large credit card company. Each year, the credit division sends a certain number of customers over to the collections division in the amount of $500M annually. About $250M is recovered annually through a phone bank at a cost of $20M. The client wants to increase that margin.
prompt.question: Question 1: How would you go about thinking about this problem? Question 2: What is the break-even point of debt recovery?

clarifying_info.q: What happens after the company contacts the customer?
clarifying_info.a: There are 3 segments of delinquent behavior: people who never pay (25%), people who pay some of the balance (50%), and people who pay all the balance (25%).

clarifying_info.q: What is the average debt per delinquent customer?
What does it cost to call a customer, and how many calls does it take?
clarifying_info.a: Cost of a call is $10; it takes an average of 20 calls to get someone to pay for those who pay something.

clarifying_info.q: Are there other collection methods available?
clarifying_info.a: It costs $200 a visit to outsource to a company that will go out and knock on doors.

clarifying_info.q: Does call yield change as more calls are made?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — as the number of calls increases, yield per call decreases.

framework: Assess current profitability: revenue recovered vs. cost of collections
Segment delinquents by likelihood and ability to pay
Analyze cost drivers: call volume, cost per call, outsourced visit costs
Identify levers to increase revenue recovery
Identify levers to decrease collection costs
Determine break-even point where marginal cost of an additional call equals marginal revenue recovered (MC = MR)

questions.prompt: Question 1: How would you approach improving the margin of the collections division?
questions.guidance: The candidate should analyze profitability (current recovery $250M on $500M portfolio at $20M cost = 46% net margin on recovered amount). To increase revenue: automate early call rounds for all delinquents to improve yield efficiency; concentrate human calls and in-person visits on customers most likely to pay all or some balance; identify high-probability payers via income/employment records and assets (higher income-to-debt ratios, white-collar jobs, substantial asset ownership). To decrease costs: outsource collections where appropriate; automation reduces costs. Segment strategy is key — do not waste resources on the 25% who never pay.

math.setup: Current state: $500M in delinquent debt sent to collections; $250M recovered; $20M cost. Net margin = ($250M - $20M) / $250M = 92% on recovered revenue, or profit = $230M.
math.answer: Current net profit on collections is $230M; cost to recover is $0.08 per dollar recovered.

questions.prompt: Question 2: What is the break-even point of debt recovery? Draw a graph showing when to stop making calls.
questions.guidance: The candidate should recognize this is a marginal analysis problem. As the number of calls increases, yield per call decreases (diminishing returns). The optimal stopping point is where marginal cost (MC) of an additional call equals marginal revenue (MR) from that call. The candidate should draw a graph with number of calls on the x-axis and dollar value on the y-axis, showing a downward-sloping MR curve and a flat or rising MC line; the intersection is the break-even/optimal stop point. Beyond that point, additional calls destroy value.

math.setup: Cost per call = $10. Average calls to collect from a paying customer = 20. Cost to collect from one paying customer via calls = 20 x $10 = $200. Average debt = $10,000. Payers-in-full (25%) and partial payers (50%) combined = 75% of delinquents.
steps: Cost to collect per paying account = 20 calls x $10/call = $200
Revenue per partial payer = some fraction of $10,000 (partial — amount not specified)
Break-even on a full-payer: $200 cost vs. $10,000 recovery — well above break-even
For call optimization: stop calling when the expected recovery from one more call < $10 (cost of that call)
Graphically: plot diminishing MR curve against flat MC=$10 line; stop at intersection
math.answer: Break-even per call is $10 in expected recovery. Stop making calls when the marginal expected recovery per call falls below $10. On a full-paying account, break-even is easily cleared ($10,000 / 20 calls = $500 expected revenue per call on average). The graph shows MC = $10 as a horizontal line and MR as a downward-sloping curve; optimum is at their intersection.

brainstorming.prompt: What additional strategies could improve the profitability of the collections division beyond optimizing call volume?

categories.name: Revenue Enhancement
ideas: Negotiate partial settlements for never-pay segment to recover something rather than nothing
Sell uncollectable debt to third-party debt buyers at a discount
Offer hardship payment plans to partial payers to convert them to full payers over time
Use data analytics to better predict which delinquents will pay and prioritize accordingly

categories.name: Cost Reduction
ideas: Automate initial contact rounds (IVR/robocall) to reduce cost per contact
Outsource low-value accounts to cheaper third-party collectors
Use digital channels (email, SMS) as lower-cost first-touch before live calls
Centralize collections operations to reduce overhead

categories.name: Segmentation & Targeting
ideas: Score delinquents by income-to-debt ratio, employment status, and asset ownership
Apply different collection strategies by segment: automation for never-pay, intensive human contact for likely-pay-all
Use credit bureau data to refresh scoring regularly
Deprioritize accounts where cost of collection exceeds expected recovery

categories.name: Process Improvement
ideas: Reduce average calls needed per account through better scripting and timing
Call at optimal times of day/week to increase contact and payment rates
Track agent performance and coach low performers

recommendation: Implement a tiered collection strategy: automate first-contact calls for all delinquents, then concentrate live agent calls and in-person visits on the 75% who are likely to pay (partial or full payers), identified via income/employment/asset data
Introduce a marginal analysis framework so the team stops calling any account once expected recovery per additional call drops below $10 (the cost per call), eliminating value-destroying call volume
risks: Misclassification of payers vs. non-payers could cause the company to abandon recoverable accounts
Outsourcing or automation may damage customer relationships for cardholders who eventually become current again
Regulatory/compliance risk in collections practices (FDCPA) must be managed carefully
next_steps: Build or license a credit scoring model to segment delinquents by payment probability
Pilot automated first-round calling and measure recovery rates vs. control group
Evaluate third-party door-knock vendors to compare ROI vs. in-house phone calls
Explore sale of never-pay debt to debt buyers to monetize the 25% currently written off
